claim: GRA16 contains a PEXEL-like motif (RRLAE) at amino acid positions 63 to 67 after the signal peptide.
source: Within the N-terminus of GRA16 (Bougdour et al., 2013), we observed a PEXEL-like motif (RRLAE) after the SP, at amino acid positions 63 to 67 (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by direct observation of the GRA16 sequence and is illustrated in Figure 1A showing the schematic representation of GRA16 with the RRLAE motif.

claim: GRA16WT-HA is represented by a strong signal at ~57 kDa and two minor species at approximately 60 kDa and 54 kDa.
source: Immunoblot analysis showed that GRA16WT-HA is represented by a strong signal at ~57 kDa and two minor species at approximately 60 kDa and 54 kDa, respectively (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B demonstrating the molecular weight species of GRA16WT-HA.

claim: Mutation of the PEXEL-like motif from RRLAE to AAAAE prevents proteolytic processing of GRA16.
source: Following mutation of the PEXEL-like motif (GRA16AAAAE-HA), the two lower molecular weight species were not observed, demonstrating that the mutated protein was no longer processed in the same way.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot analysis comparing GRA16WT-HA and GRA16AAAAE-HA, showing loss of processing in the mutant.

claim: GRA16AAAAE-HA protein levels are dramatically reduced compared to GRA16WT-HA despite both being expressed from the endogenous locus.
source: Interestingly, while both proteins were expressed from the endogenous locus, the amount of GRA16AAAAE-HA protein was dramatically reduced (Figure 1B), suggesting the mutant protein was degraded in the absence of appropriate N-terminal processing.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1B showing reduced protein levels of the mutant, with inference about degradation.

claim: GRA16WT-HA is exported into the host cell where it accumulates in the nucleus.
source: GRA16WT-HA was observed within the host cell nucleus, as previously reported (Bougdour et al., 2013), as well as at the PV and within parasites (Figure 1C-i).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence assay data shown in Figure 1C-i and is consistent with previous published work.

claim: GRA16AAAAE-HA export to the host cell is severely impaired compared to GRA16WT-HA.
source: In contrast, GRA16AAAAE-HA was observed either within parasites, in small punctate structures reminiscent of the Golgi or in the PV space between parasites (Figure 1C-ii). In a minority of cells, a small amount of exported GRA16AAAAE-HA could be observed within the host nuclei (Figure 1C-ii, panel 2); however, there was a large and clear defect in export in the mutant line.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1C-ii showing altered localization of the mutant protein.

claim: The PEXEL-like motif is required for correct proteolytic processing of GRA16 and efficient export to the host cell.
source: Taken together, this demonstrates that the PEXEL-like motif is required for correct proteolytic processing of GRA16 and efficient export to the host cell.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on GRA16 processing and localization.

claim: The PEXEL-like motif in Toxoplasma is termed the Toxoplasma export element (TEXEL).
source: We therefore termed this motif the Toxoplasma export element (TEXEL).
evidence: The claim is a nomenclature decision based on the functional characterization of the motif.

claim: ASP5 (TGME49_242720) is the top BLAST hit when searching ToxoDB using P. falciparum PMV as a query.
source: We searched ToxoDB (http://toxodb.org) using P. falciparum PMV (PfPMV) as a query and the top Basic Local Alignment Search Tool (BLAST) hit was aspartyl protease 5 (ASP5, TGME49_242720), consistent with previous phylogenetic analysis of this group of proteases in Apicomplexa (Shea et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by BLAST search results and is consistent with previous phylogenetic analysis.

claim: ASP5 and P. falciparum PMV share approximately 33% similarity and 14% identity across the full-length alignment.
source: An alignment of the two proteins revealed that they share approximately 33% similarity and 14% identity across the full-length alignment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ASP5 and PMV share several key features including an N-terminal signal peptide, a core aspartyl protease domain with DTG and DSG catalytic dyad residues, a plant-like nepenthesin fold, and a C-terminal transmembrane domain.
source: The proteins shared several key features, including an N-terminal SP, a core aspartyl protease domain (with DTG and DSG residues defining the catalytic dyad), a plant-like nepenthesin fold, as well as a C-terminal transmembrane domain (Hodder et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and comparison with known structural features, citing previous work.

claim: ASP5 contains a significantly longer signal peptide and C-terminal tail sequence than PMV.
source: While ASP5 contains a significantly longer SP and C-terminal tail sequence than PfPMV, it lacks the helix-turn-helix motif found in PMV from all Plasmodium spp. that is hypothesized to interact with other ER proteins (Hodder et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence comparison between ASP5 and PMV.

claim: ASP5 lacks the helix-turn-helix motif found in PMV from all Plasmodium species.
source: While ASP5 contains a significantly longer SP and C-terminal tail sequence than PfPMV, it lacks the helix-turn-helix motif found in PMV from all Plasmodium spp. that is hypothesized to interact with other ER proteins (Hodder et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence comparison and structural analysis.

claim: ASP5WT-HA3 is present as two major species of approximately 90 and 55 kDa.
source: Immunoblot analysis with anti-HA antibodies revealed ASP5WT-HA3 is present as two major species of approximately 90 and 55 kDa (Figure 2A), consistent with a signal peptidase-cleaved species and possibly an activated form, respectively (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ASP5MUT-HA3 (D431A, D682A) is observed predominantly as the ~90 kDa form, suggesting that ASP5 may auto-activate to produce the ~55 kDa species.
source: A mutant form of ASP5, where the conserved aspartic acid catalytic residues were mutated to alanine (ASP5D431A, D682A-HA3; herein referred to as ASP5MUT-HA3), was observed predominantly as the ~90 kDa form, suggesting that ASP5 may auto-activate to produce the ~55 kDa species (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data comparing wild-type and mutant ASP5, with inference about auto-activation.

claim: ASP5WT-HA3 localizes to the Golgi and co-localizes with the Golgi marker GalNAc-YFP.
source: Using immunofluorescence microscopy with anti-HA antibodies, we observed ASP5WT-HA3 in apical puncta that co-localized with GalNAc-YFP, a known Golgi marker (Nishi et al., 2008) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B demonstrating co-localization with a known Golgi marker.

claim: ASP5MUT-HA3 localizes to discrete puncta adjacent to the nucleus, representative of the Golgi.
source: ASP5MUT-HA3 also localized to discrete puncta adjacent to the nucleus, representative of the Golgi (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Immunoprecipitated ASP5WT-HA3 cleaves the GRA16 TEXEL peptide (DABCYL-R-VSRRLAEEP-E-EDANS).
source: Immunoprecipitated ASP5WT-HA3, but not ASP5MUT-HA3, cleaves GRA16 TEXEL (DABCYL-R-VSRRLAEEP-E-EDANS) but not the RRL>AAA peptide.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorogenic peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Immunoprecipitated ASP5MUT-HA3 does not cleave the GRA16 TEXEL peptide.
source: Immunoprecipitated ASP5WT-HA3, but not ASP5MUT-HA3, cleaves GRA16 TEXEL (DABCYL-R-VSRRLAEEP-E-EDANS) but not the RRL>AAA peptide.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorogenic peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ASP5WT-HA3 does not cleave the GRA16 TEXEL peptide when the RRL motif is mutated to AAA.
source: Immunoprecipitated ASP5WT-HA3, but not ASP5MUT-HA3, cleaves GRA16 TEXEL (DABCYL-R-VSRRLAEEP-E-EDANS) but not the RRL>AAA peptide.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorogenic peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ASP5 cleaves the GRA16 TEXEL peptide after the leucine residue (RxL↓xE/Q/D).
source: Peptides incubated in buffer alone remained intact in contrast to peptides incubated with ASP5WT-HA3, which resulted in the generation of a product corresponding to processing within the TEXEL after leucine (DABCYL-R-VSRRL↓). This processing event after the leucine residue, hereafter referred to as the P1 position, is the identical site of processing of the PEXEL by PMV in both P. falciparum and P. vivax (Boddey et al., 2009; 2010; Russo et al., 2010; Sleebs et al., 2014b).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 2D identifying the cleavage site.

claim: ASP5WT-HA3 efficiently cleaves the GRA16 peptide with Km 47.8 ± 18.4 μM.
source: ASP5WT-HA3 efficiently cleaved the GRA16 peptide with Km 47.8 ± 18.4 μM (mean ± SD) (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: ASP5WT-HA3 activity is optimal at pH 5.5.
source: ASP5WT-HA3 activity was optimal at pH 5.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), in contrast to pH 6.4 for PMV (Boddey et al., 2010; Russo et al., 2010), consistent with the Golgi being a more acidic environment than the ER (Wu et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by pH optimization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The optimal pH for ASP5 activity (pH 5.5) is consistent with the Golgi being a more acidic environment than the ER.
source: ASP5WT-HA3 activity was optimal at pH 5.5 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), in contrast to pH 6.4 for PMV (Boddey et al., 2010; Russo et al., 2010), consistent with the Golgi being a more acidic environment than the ER (Wu et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of pH optima and known pH differences between organelles.

claim: WEHI-586 (RRLStatine) inhibits ASP5WT-HA3 with IC50 of 63 ± 15 nM.
source: Incubation of ASP5WT-HA3 with WEHI-586 blocked cleavage of the GRA16 peptide with IC50 of 63 ± 15 nM (mean ± standard error of the mean) (Figure 2F), demonstrating the potent affinity of the TEXEL sequence for ASP5.
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response inhibition data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: ASP5 is a Golgi-resident protease that cleaves the GRA16 TEXEL motif after the leucine residue.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that ASP5 is a Golgi-resident protease that cleaves the GRA16 TEXEL motif after the leucine residue and can be potently inhibited by a TEXEL-mimetic small molecule.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on localization, cleavage site, and inhibition data.

claim: PfPMV-HA cleaves peptides containing the wild-type KAHRP PEXEL but not P3 (R>K) or P1 (L>I) point mutations.
source: PfPMV-HA behaved as expected (Boddey et al., 2010; 2013), cleaving peptides containing the WT KAHRP PEXEL but not P3 (R>K) or P1 (L>I) point mutations (Figure 3A-i).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3A-i and is consistent with previous publications.

claim: PfPMV-HA cleaves the GRA16 TEXEL peptide with notably higher efficiency than it cleaves the KAHRP PEXEL peptide.
source: This Plasmodium enzyme also cleaved the peptide containing the WT GRA16 TEXEL, with notably higher efficiency than it cleaved the peptide KAHRP; however, it did not cleave GRA16 peptides containing TEXEL mutations at P3 (R>A) or P1 (L>A), as expected based on the known specificity of this protease (Figure 3A-i).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparative peptide cleavage data shown in Figure 3A-i.

claim: ASP5 cleaves the GRA16 TEXEL peptide but does not cleave peptides containing mutations at P3 (R>A) or P1 (L>A).
source: Similarly, ASP5 cleaved the GRA16 TEXEL peptide but did not cleave peptides containing mutations of the TEXEL, P3 (R>A) or P1 (L>A), demonstrating that the P3 and P1 positions of the substrate (i.e. arginine and leucine, respectively) are important for ASP5 activity, as is the case for PMV (Figure 3A-ii) (Boddey et al., 2010; Russo et al., 2010; Sleebs et al., 2014b).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3A-ii.

claim: ASP5 does not cleave KAHRP PEXEL peptides above background levels.
source: In contrast to PMV, ASP5 did not cleave KAHRP peptides above background levels (Figure 3A-ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3A-ii.

claim: Replacement of the P2 residue in the KAHRP PEXEL (threonine) with arginine (P2 T>R) results in a 3-fold increase in cleavage by ASP5.
source: Replacement of the P2 residue in the KAHRP PEXEL (threonine) with the corresponding residue in GRA16 (arginine) (i.e. P2 T>R) resulted in a 3-fold increase in cleavage, demonstrating the importance of the P2 position for ASP5 activity, although cleavage of this peptide was still well below that seen for the native GRA16 TEXEL peptide (Figure 3A-ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3A-ii.

claim: ASP5 and PMV both cleave peptides containing RxL sequences but do not share identical substrate specificity.
source: This demonstrates that while ASP5 and PMV both cleave peptides containing RxL sequences, they do not share identical substrate specificity.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from comparative peptide cleavage data.

claim: ASP5 does not well tolerate conservative and non-conservative changes at the P1, P2 or P3 positions.
source: This demonstrated that ASP5 does not well tolerate conservative and non-conservative changes at the P1, P2 or P3 positions.
evidence: The claim is supported by point mutation analysis of the GRA16 TEXEL substrate.

claim: ASP5 can cleave RKL at approximately 35-40% of wild-type activity.
source: It appeared that ASP5 could cleave RKL at ~35–40% of WT, yet the physiological relevance of this is not known (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mutation of the GRA16 TEXEL P2' residue E>A results in enhanced processing by ASP5.
source: Interestingly, mutation of the GRA16 TEXEL P2' residue E>A resulted in enhanced processing, illustrating that this position in ASP5 substrates may not be essential for activity, similar to PMV, but can alter cleavage efficiency (Boddey et al., 2009; 2010; Sleebs et al., 2014a; 2014b).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data and comparison with PMV.

claim: ASP5 cleaves the wild-type GRA19 TEXEL peptide (RRLSD) efficiently.
source: The WT GRA19 TEXEL peptide was processed efficiently and this was inhibited when the TEXEL was mutated from RRL to AAA (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ASP5 does not process the RELLD sequence in GRA21.
source: In contrast, the RELLD sequence in GRA21, and the corresponding AAALD mutant, were not processed by ASP5 (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: ASP5 likely processes GRA21 at the RRLAE position, which is the same sequence as the TEXEL in GRA16.
source: Since the RRLAE in the N-terminus of GRA21 is the same sequence as the TEXEL in GRA16, it is highly likely that ASP5 processes GRA21 at this position.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on sequence similarity and known ASP5 specificity.

claim: ASP5 has a relatively strict requirement for arginine at P3 and P2, and leucine at P1 of its substrates.
source: Taken together, this work demonstrates that ASP5 has relatively strict requirement for arginine at P3 and P2, and leucine at P1 of its substrates (Figure 3D), and that residues at P1' and P2' are dispensable for processing but can influence the efficiency of cleavage by this enzyme.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on peptide cleavage data and is illustrated in Figure 3D.

claim: Residues at P1' and P2' are dispensable for ASP5 processing but can influence the efficiency of cleavage.
source: Taken together, this work demonstrates that ASP5 has relatively strict requirement for arginine at P3 and P2, and leucine at P1 of its substrates (Figure 3D), and that residues at P1' and P2' are dispensable for processing but can influence the efficiency of cleavage by this enzyme.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on peptide cleavage data.

claim: The guanidyl side-chain of arginine at P3 of the GRA16 TEXEL forms interactions with the side-chains of E506 and Q549 in ASP5.
source: The model shows that the guanidyl side-chain of arginine at P3 (the first position in the TEXEL sequence) forms interactions with the side-chains of E506 and Q549 in a manner completely analogous to that observed in the structure of PMV in complex with the statine inhibitor, WEHI-842 (Hodder et al., 2015) (Figure 3E-i).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 3E-i.

claim: The leucine at P1 of the TEXEL is surrounded by hydrophobic residues I429, Y503, F546 and I554 of ASP5.
source: Furthermore, the leucine at P1 of the TEXEL is surrounded by hydrophobic residues I429, Y503, F546 and I554 of ASP5; the isoleucine at position 554 in ASP5 is a valine in PMV, while the other residues, I, Y, F are identical between ASP5 and PMV (Figure 3E-i).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 3E-i.

claim: The AutoDock potential predicts that ASP5 binds the GRA16 peptide (SRRLAEE) 5 kJ/mol more tightly than an SRTLAEE mutant form.
source: This was supported using our model, as the AutoDock potential predicted that ASP5 binds the GRA16 peptide (SRRLAEE) 5 kJ/mol more tightly than an SRTLAEE mutant form of GRA16 (Figure 3E-ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling data shown in Figure 3E-ii.

claim: The guanidine side-chain of arginine at P2 of native GRA16 forms hydrogen bonds with the side-chain hydroxyl of S505 and the backbone carbonyl of A776 in ASP5.
source: The guanidine side-chain of arginine at P2 of native GRA16 forms hydrogen bonds with the side-chain hydroxyl of S505 and the backbone carbonyl of A776 (Figure 3E-i), whereas the mutated GRA16 substrate containing threonine at P2 forms only a single hydrogen bond with the side-chain hydroxyl of S505 (Figure 3E-ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural modeling data shown in Figure 3E-i.

claim: The differences in hydrogen bonding between arginine and threonine at P2 account for approximately 50% of the total difference in calculated binding affinity between the two substrates.
source: Taken together, these differences in binding interactions accounts for ~50% of the total difference in the calculated binding affinity between the two substrates, providing a clear structural explanation for the substrate specificity (i.e. RRL) observed for ASP5.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational analysis of binding energies from the structural model.

claim: Mutation of leucine at P1 of the GRA16 TEXEL to valine reduces the calculated binding energy by 6 kJ/mol.
source: Mutation of leucine at P1 of the GRA16 TEXEL to valine reduces the calculated binding energy by 6 kJ/mol, which is in line with our observations that mutations at this position significantly reduce ASP5 activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling and is consistent with experimental data.

claim: Mutation of alanine at P1' to valine is predicted to slightly increase the binding energy by less than 1 kJ/mol.
source: Mutation of alanine at P1' (position 4 of the GRA16 TEXEL, RRLAE) to valine is predicted to slightly increase the binding energy, but by less than 1 kJ/mol.
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling.

claim: Mutation of glutamine at P2' to alanine causes an 11 kJ/mol reduction in calculated binding affinity in the model.
source: Interestingly, mutation of glutamine at P2' (position 5 of the GRA16 TEXEL) to alanine causes an 11 kJ/mol reduction in calculated binding affinity in the model, in contrast to the increase in ASP5 activity observed in vitro (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by computational modeling, though it contrasts with experimental data.

claim: The ASP5 gene was successfully disrupted using a double homologous recombination strategy combined with an ASP5-targeted CRISPR approach.
source: Utilizing a double homologous recombination strategy combined with an ASP5-targeted CRISPR approach, we were able to successfully disrupt the ASP5 gene, where the 3' flank underwent homologous recombination, while apparent lack of NotI cleavage and the presence of a Cas9-induced cut site resulted in the whole plasmid integrating non-homologously at that site, meaning that a green fluorescent protein (GFP) expression cassette also integrated (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-i).
evidence: The claim is supported by PCR and sequencing data confirming the gene disruption.

claim: Δasp5 parasites produce smaller plaques than wild-type parasites in a 7-day plaque assay.
source: To determine overall qualitative changes in asexual growth rate, WT and Δasp5 tachyzoites were grown for 7 days in a plaque assay (Figure 4A-i) and we observed that the plaques of the Δasp5 parasites were smaller than those generated by WT parasites, demonstrating that Δasp5 parasites have a clear growth disadvantage under simple in vitro growth conditions.
evidence: The claim is supported by plaque assay data shown in Figure 4A-i.

claim: The growth defect of Δasp5 parasites is restored following complementation with a stably-integrated copy of ASP5.
source: This defect was restored following complementation with a stably-integrated copy of ASP5 (Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3) driven from the tubulin promoter (Figure 4A-ii.)
evidence: The claim is supported by plaque assay data shown in Figure 4A-ii.

claim: Δasp5CRISPR tachyzoites have no major difference in intracellular replication compared to wild-type or Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 parasites at 16 hours post infection.
source: From this analysis, it is clear that Δasp5CRISPR tachyzoites have no major difference in intracellular replication to either WT or Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 parasites.
evidence: The claim is supported by replication assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The smaller plaque size of Δasp5CRISPR tachyzoites is not due to retardation in replication.
source: This suggests that smaller plaque size of Δasp5CRISPR tachyzoites, compared to WT and Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 parasites, is not due to retardation in replication.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the replication assay data.

claim: In Δasp5 parasites, GRA16-HA migrates as a larger protein that has not been processed correctly.
source: Western blot analysis of GRA16-HA in otherwise WT parasites yielded the same three bands as seen in Figure 1B, consistent with cleavage within the TEXEL motif, whereas in the Δasp5 parasites, GRA16-HA migrated as a larger protein that had not been processed correctly, mirroring the GRA16AAAAE-HA profile (Figure 4C, Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: GRA16-HA is no longer exported into the host cell during infection with Δasp5 parasites.
source: While GRA16-HA produced by WT parasites was observed in the host nucleus as expected, this effector was no longer exported into the host cell during infection with Δasp5 parasites and instead appeared to localize to an internal structure reminiscent of the Golgi and in the PV space (Figure 4D), similar to the GRA16AAAAE-HA mutant (Figure 1C-ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Processing by ASP5 is essential for correct trafficking of GRA16 from the parasite into the infected host cell.
source: This confirms that processing by ASP5 is essential for correct trafficking of GRA16 from the parasite into the infected host cell.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the processing and localization data of GRA16 in wild-type and Δasp5 parasites.

claim: Toxoplasma tachyzoites actively induce expression of host c-Myc following infection.
source: It has recently been shown that Toxoplasma tachyzoites, but not the related Neospora species, actively induce expression of host c-Myc following infection (Franco et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous work.

claim: Activation of c-Myc by Toxoplasma was not induced in response to parasite invasion or injection of rhoptry proteins.
source: This activation of c-Myc was not induced in response to parasite invasion or injection of rhoptry proteins (Franco et al., 2014), suggesting that one or more dense granule proteins may be responsible.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation of previous work and inference about dense granule proteins.

claim: HFFs infected with Δasp5 parasites express approximately 6.4-fold less c-Myc than those infected with wild-type parasites.
source: Quantification by IFA showed that HFFs infected with parasites lacking ASP5 expressed approximately 6.4-fold less c-Myc than those infected with WT parasites (normalized ratio of c-Myc to 4',6-diamidino-2-phenylindole [DAPI]) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: ASP5 is required for Toxoplasma to induce c-Myc in infected cells.
source: To confirm this, c-Myc induction was measured by immunoblot of whole cell protein fractions. While c-Myc expression was induced in host cells infected with WT parasites, the signal was dramatically reduced in HFFs infected with the same number of Δasp5 parasites (Figure 5C), confirming that ASP5 is required for Toxoplasma to induce c-Myc in infected cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The up-regulation of c-Myc induced by tachyzoites is controlled by one or more ASP5-dependent proteins.
source: Together, this work suggests that the up-regulation of c-Myc induced by tachyzoites is controlled by one or more ASP5-dependent proteins.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the requirement of ASP5 for c-Myc induction.

claim: MYR1 is processed approximately two-thirds along its sequence, revealing a C-terminal fragment that migrates at ~32 kDa and an N-terminal fragment that migrates at ~80 kDa.
source: Very recently, a novel dense granule protein was identified by the Boothroyd laboratory that localizes to the PV and is processed approximately two-thirds along its sequence, revealing a C-terminal fragment that migrates at ~32 kDa and an N-terminal fragment that migrates at ~80 kDa (Figure 6A) (Franco et al., in press).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data and citation of work in press.

claim: MYR1 contains a TEXEL-like RRLSE sequence approximately 230 residues from the C-terminus.
source: Analysis of this protein, MYR1 (TGGT1_254470), revealed a TEXEL-like RRLSE sequence approximately 230 residues from the C-terminus, the approximate position where cleavage is predicted to occur (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence analysis and schematic representation in Figure 6C.

claim: In Δasp5 mutants, MYR1 is no longer processed and instead migrates at ~105 kDa.
source: In the Δasp5 mutants, MYR1 is no longer processed and instead migrates at ~105 kDa (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ASP5 is required for cleavage of MYR1.
source: This strongly suggests that ASP5 is required for cleavage of MYR1.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the loss of MYR1 processing in Δasp5 parasites.

claim: ASP5WT-HA3 efficiently cleaves the MYR1 TEXEL peptide (RRLSE), similar to the GRA16 RRLAE control.
source: We found that ASP5WT-HA3 efficiently cleaved the MYR1 TEXEL peptide, similar to the GRA16 RRLAE control, whereas mutations of the conserved RRL residues abolished this activity (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The P1' residue (serine in MYR1 vs. alanine in GRA16) is not as constrained as the P1-3 positions for ASP5 activity.
source: This demonstrates that MYR1 contains a TEXEL sequence that can be processed by ASP5. It also suggests that the P1' residue, which naturally differs between GRA16 (alanine) and MYR1 (serine), is not as constrained as the P1-3 positions, and confirms that the P2' residue is not essential for processing, since the MYR1 TEXEL P2' (E>A) mutant peptide was efficiently processed.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on comparison of MYR1 and GRA16 TEXEL cleavage.

claim: Mutation of the MYR1 TEXEL from RRLSE to ARLSE or ARASA prevents cleavage in vivo.
source: While ectopic expression of the C-terminally tagged MYR1WT-HA resulted in detection of the expected ~32 kDa species, mutation of either RRLSE>ARLSE or RRLSE>ARASA prevented cleavage, leaving only the unprocessed species migrating at ~105 kDa (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The RRLSE sequence of MYR1 is necessary for processing in parasites.
source: Thus, this sequence of MYR1 is necessary for processing in parasites.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the mutagenesis data.

claim: ASP5 cleaves the TEXEL motif of MYR1.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that ASP5 cleaves the TEXEL motif of MYR1, and that the TEXEL can function in a novel location near the C-terminus of the protein, in contrast to Plasmodium spp. where all known PEXEL sequences are located ~15–30 amino acids from the SP cleavage site (Sargeant et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on in vitro and in vivo cleavage data.

claim: The TEXEL can function in a novel location near the C-terminus of the protein, in contrast to Plasmodium PEXEL sequences.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that ASP5 cleaves the TEXEL motif of MYR1, and that the TEXEL can function in a novel location near the C-terminus of the protein, in contrast to Plasmodium spp. where all known PEXEL sequences are located ~15–30 amino acids from the SP cleavage site (Sargeant et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the location of the TEXEL in MYR1 compared to known PEXEL locations.

claim: The percentage of the PVM associated with host mitochondria is reduced by 4.3-fold in Δasp5 parasites compared to wild-type.
source: Quantification of HMA by TEM showed that the percentage of the PVM associated with host mitochondria was reduced by 4.3-fold in Δasp5 parasites (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative TEM data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Δasp5CRISPR parasites exhibit reduced host mitochondrial association compared to wild-type parasites.
source: In contrast, Δasp5CRISPR  parasites exhibited reduced HMA, and MAF1 was incorrectly localized, appearing predominantly in punctate structures rather than at the PVM (Figure 7C, panels 2–4).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 parasites exhibit correct trafficking of MAF1 and recruitment of host mitochondria to the PVM.
source: In contrast, the Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 parasites exhibited correct trafficking of MAF1 and recruitment of host mitochondria to the PVM, which was validated in two independent complemented clones that expressed ASP5 at levels close to the endogenous expression of the enzyme (Figure 7C, panels 5–6, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7C and Western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: There are no differences in MAF1 expression or processing between wild-type and Δasp5 parasites by Western blot.
source: There were no differences in MAF1 expression or processing between the two lines by Western blot (Figure 7D), consistent with a lack of any TEXEL motif within MAF1.
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The function of MAF1 is not directly dependent on ASP5, but rather, ASP5 may act on as yet unidentified protein(s) that interact with MAF1 to facilitate efficient host mitochondrial association.
source: This result suggests that the function of MAF1 is not directly dependent on ASP5, but rather, ASP5 may act on as yet unidentified protein(s) that interact with MAF1 to facilitate efficient HMA.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the lack of MAF1 processing changes and the observed HMA defect.

claim: The nanotubular network in Δasp5 vacuoles is vastly diminished and disorganized compared to wild-type.
source: Vacuoles containing WT parasites displayed extensive structures, extending from near the posterior of parasites to the PVM, typical of the NTN (Figure 7E-i and ii). In stark contrast, the NTN in Δasp5 vacuoles was vastly diminished and disorganized in all cells examined, suggesting that one or more components involved in the biogenesis of this network requires processing by ASP5 (Figure 7E-iii and iv).
evidence: The claim is supported by TEM data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: One or more components involved in the biogenesis of the nanotubular network require processing by ASP5.
source: In stark contrast, the NTN in Δasp5 vacuoles was vastly diminished and disorganized in all cells examined, suggesting that one or more components involved in the biogenesis of this network requires processing by ASP5 (Figure 7E-iii and iv).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the NTN defect observed in Δasp5 parasites.

claim: Export of GRA24-Myc3 is completely blocked in Δasp5 parasites.
source: GRA24-Myc3 was expressed in parasites and exported to the host cell nucleus by WT parasites as previously described (Braun et al., 2013); however, export was completely blocked in Δasp5 parasites (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Complementation of Δasp5 parasites with ASP5WT-HA3 restores the export of GRA24-Myc3.
source: Complementation of Δasp5 parasites with ASP5WT-HA3 restored the export of GRA24-Myc3 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Assessment of GRA24-Myc3 processing by Western blot did not reveal any size difference between wild-type and Δasp5 parasites.
source: Despite the requirement of ASP5 for GRA24 export, assessment of processing by Western blot did not reveal any size difference in GRA24-Myc3 between WT and Δasp5 parasites (Figure 8B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: ASP5 does not efficiently cleave peptides containing non-canonical TEXEL-like sequences from GRA24 (RGYHG, RGGLQ, RSLGM).
source: While GRA24 lacks a canonical TEXEL sequence (RRLxx), it does contain the non-canonical TEXEL-like sequences RGYHG, RGGLQ and RSLGM, and so we assessed whether these might be cleaved by ASP5 using synthetic peptides; however, none were efficiently processed (Figure 8C).
evidence: The claim is supported by peptide cleavage assay data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: GRA24 is not a direct substrate of ASP5 but its export is dependent on this protease.
source: Collectively, this suggests that GRA24 is not a direct substrate of ASP5 but its export is dependent on this protease.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the lack of GRA24 processing and the inability of ASP5 to cleave GRA24 peptides, despite export being ASP5-dependent.

claim: At a false discovery rate of 5%, 3402 genes were significantly up-regulated and 3369 genes were significantly down-regulated in response to wild-type infection.
source: At a false discovery rate of 5%, 3402 genes were significantly up-regulated and 3369 genes were significantly down-regulated in response to the WT infection, whereas only 1033 genes were significantly up- and 817 were significantly down-regulated in response to Δasp5 parasites.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Only 1033 genes were significantly up-regulated and 817 were significantly down-regulated in response to Δasp5 parasite infection.
source: At a false discovery rate of 5%, 3402 genes were significantly up-regulated and 3369 genes were significantly down-regulated in response to the WT infection, whereas only 1033 genes were significantly up- and 817 were significantly down-regulated in response to Δasp5 parasites.
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis.

claim: Of the 3402 genes up-regulated during wild-type infection, only 862 (25%) remained significantly up-regulated upon deletion of ASP5.
source: Of the 3402 genes up-regulated during WT infection, only 862 (25% ) remained significantly up-regulated upon deletion of ASP5 (Figure 9A-ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 9A-ii.

claim: Of the 3269 genes down-regulated during wild-type infection, only 742 (22%) remained significantly down-regulated upon deletion of ASP5.
source: Of the 3269 genes down-regulated during WT infection, only 742 (22%) remained significantly down-regulated upon deletion of ASP5 (Figure 9A-ii).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq differential expression analysis shown in Figure 9A-ii.

claim: The log-fold change during infection with Δasp5 parasites was, on average, only 60% of the log-fold change during infection with wild-type parasites.
source: The log-fold change during infection with Δasp5 parasites was, on average, only 60% of the log-fold change during infection with WT parasites (Figure 9A-i).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 9A-i.

claim: Most genes responding to parasite infection do so, at least partly, due to an ASP5-dependent pathway.
source: This suggests that most genes responding to parasite infection do so, at least partly, due to an ASP5-dependent pathway.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the reduced magnitude of transcriptional changes in Δasp5 infection.

claim: ASP5 controls the up-regulation of gene sets implicated in cell cycle, nucleic acid metabolism and binding, nucleopore association and chromatin binding.
source: We observed that ASP5 controlled the up-regulation of gene sets implicated in cell cycle, nucleic acid metabolism and binding, nucleopore association and chromatin binding.
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Table 1.

claim: ASP5 plays a key role in the down-regulation of genes implicated in autophagy, peroxisome fission, vacuole organization, protein trafficking (i.e. syntaxin binding) and intracellular signaling processes.
source: Furthermore, ASP5 played a key role in the down-regulation of genes implicated in autophagy, peroxisome fission, vacuole organization, protein trafficking (i.e. syntaxin binding) and intracellular signaling processes (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Table 1.

claim: ASP5-dependent pathways play an important role in controlling specific cellular processes that may facilitate parasite persistence within the cell.
source: This outlines that ASP5-dependent pathways play an important role in controlling specific cellular processes that may facilitate parasite persistence within the cell.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the Gene Ontology analysis results.

claim: The transcriptional profile of Δgra16 parasite infection is strongly correlated with the transcriptional profile observed in Δasp5 parasite infection.
source: We found that the transcriptional profile of Δgra16 parasite infection is strongly correlated with the transcriptional profile that we observed in Δasp5 parasite infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNA-seq data with published Δgra16 data.

claim: Genes up-regulated in the Δasp5 parasite infection were strongly enriched for up-regulated Δgra16 genes (ROAST P-value = 5×10–5).
source: Genes up-regulated in the Δasp5 parasite infection were strongly enriched for up-regulated Δgra16 genes, and similarly, the down-regulated Δasp5 were strongly enriched for Δgra16 genes (ROAST P-value =5×10–5).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene set enrichment analysis comparing Δasp5 and Δgra16 transcriptional profiles.

claim: Transcriptional changes induced by GRA16 mostly represent a subset of all genes influenced by ASP5.
source: This shows that transcriptional changes induced by GRA16 mostly represent a subset of all genes influenced by ASP5.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the enrichment analysis comparing Δgra16 and Δasp5 transcriptional profiles.

claim: All mice infected with either wild-type or Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 tachyzoites (15 ± 3 live parasites) succumbed to infection by day 8.
source: Over a 20-day period, we found that all mice infected with either WT or Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 tachyzoites succumbed to infection by day 8 and dropped weight accordingly (Figure 10A).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse survival data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: All mice infected with Δasp5CRISPR parasites (15 ± 3 live parasites) were still alive at day 20, maintained body weight and appeared healthy.
source: Strikingly, all mice infected with Δasp5CRISPR parasites were still alive at day 20, they maintained body weight and appeared healthy, despite sero-converting by day 14 (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse survival and body weight data shown in Figure 10A and seroconversion data in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mice previously injected with Δasp5CRISPR parasites were protected from death upon re-challenge with 200 wild-type parasites (~50 live parasites).
source: We also confirmed prior infection by performing a re-challenge experiment, where mice were injected with 200 wild-type parasites, equating to ~50 live parasites (as determined by plaque assay). While 'naïve' PBS (vehicle)-injected mice succumbed to infection by day 10, all those previously injected with Δasp5CRISPRall survived and maintained normal body weight (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse re-challenge survival data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: All mice infected with wild-type or Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 tachyzoites (~50 live parasites) succumbed to infection by day 10.
source: All mice infected with wild type or Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 tachyzoites succumbed to infection by day 10, whereas those injected with Δasp5CRISPR parasites exhibited a delay to death, including one mouse that survived the experiment and was seropositive for anti-Toxoplasma antibodies when tested at day 14 (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse survival data shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Mice injected with Δasp5CRISPR parasites (~50 live parasites) exhibited a delay to death, with one mouse surviving the 15-day experiment.
source: All mice infected with wild type or Δasp5CRISPR:ASP5WT-HA3 tachyzoites succumbed to infection by day 10, whereas those injected with Δasp5CRISPR parasites exhibited a delay to death, including one mouse that survived the experiment and was seropositive for anti-Toxoplasma antibodies when tested at day 14 (Figure 10—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by mouse survival data shown in Figure 10C and seroconversion data in Figure 10—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ASP5-deficient tachyzoites exhibit attenuation even in the hypervirulent RH strain at a dose of 50 parasites.
source: Thus, ASP5-deficient tachyzoites exhibit attenuation even in the hypervirulent RH strain at a dose of 50 parasites, while injection with 15 parasites resulted in parasite clearance and provided protective immunity following re-challenge with a lethal dose of wild type tachyzoites.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the mouse virulence data.

claim: Injection with 15 ASP5-deficient parasites resulted in parasite clearance and provided protective immunity following re-challenge with a lethal dose of wild-type tachyzoites.
source: Thus, ASP5-deficient tachyzoites exhibit attenuation even in the hypervirulent RH strain at a dose of 50 parasites, while injection with 15 parasites resulted in parasite clearance and provided protective immunity following re-challenge with a lethal dose of wild type tachyzoites.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the mouse virulence and re-challenge data.

claim: The ASP5-dependent export pathway is necessary for virulence of Toxoplasma in a mouse model.
source: This work strongly suggests that the ASP5-dependent export pathway is necessary for virulence of Toxoplasma in a mouse model.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the mouse virulence studies.

claim: ASP5 is the first identified component of the dense granule export machinery in Toxoplasma.
source: Here, we identify the novel Golgi-resident aspartyl protease 5 (ASP5) that is the first known component of the dense granule export machinery in Toxoplasma.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a major finding of the study.

claim: ASP5 controls establishment of the nanotubular network.
source: Furthermore, ASP5 controls establishment of the nanotubular network and is required for the efficient recruitment of host mitochondria to the vacuole.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by TEM data.

claim: ASP5 is required for the efficient recruitment of host mitochondria to the vacuole.
source: Furthermore, ASP5 controls establishment of the nanotubular network and is required for the efficient recruitment of host mitochondria to the vacuole.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by TEM and immunofluorescence data.

claim: The ASP5-dependent pathway influences thousands of the transcriptional changes that Toxoplasma imparts on its host cell.
source: Assessment of host gene expression reveals that the ASP5-dependent pathway influences thousands of the transcriptional changes that Toxoplasma imparts on its host cell.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Loss of ASP5 results in attenuation of virulence of tachyzoites in vivo.
source: All these changes result in attenuation of virulence of Δasp5 tachyzoites in vivo.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and supported by mouse virulence studies.

claim: This work characterizes the first identified machinery required for export of Toxoplasma effectors into the infected host cell.
source: This work characterizes the first identified machinery required for export of Toxoplasma effectors into the infected host cell.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract as a summary of the study's significance.
